The highly threatened chimpanzee subspecies, the Western Chimpanzee, whose population trend overall is on the decline, occurs in the Gola-Tiwai Complex at comparatively higher densities than elsewhere and is one of just seven exceptionally stable or high Western chimpanzee density sites and is an important area for the survival of the subspecies. The Greater Gola Landscape, of which the Gola-Tiwai Complex is part, is also a stronghold for the equally threatened Forest Elephant in west Africa. The rich bird fauna of the Gola-Tiwai Complex includes up to 448 species including globally important populations of the White-breasted Guineafowl, the Timneh Parrot and the flagship White-necked Rockfowl which nests on rock faces under the forest canopy and whose survival in this landscape may be due in part to its cultural significance for the local Mende people. Thanks to its steep slopes and rocky outcrops, the Gola-Tiwai Complex includes an abundance of habitats suitable for nests of the White-necked Rockfowl. Invertebrates include over 500 species of butterfly and 140 species of dragonflies and damselflies. Integrity The majority of the Gola-Tiwai Complex consists of primary moist or semi-deciduous tropical rainforest that has never been commercially exploited. The remaining area consists of secondary vegetation that is regenerating naturally since commercial timber extraction and shifting cultivation ended in 2003. Deforestation rates are low compared to the Upper Guinean Forest more broadly. The four component parts that constitute the Gola-Tiwai Complex are sufficiently large together, and ecological connectivity between them sufficiently intact, to maintain viable populations of all but the widest-ranging species. Inventories and monitoring conducted at Gola and Tiwai since the 1980s indicate that all the species that would be expected in a block of Upper Guinean Forest in this location are present and their populations stable. Activities within the formal buffer zone and the sustainable collection of non-timber forest products within the protected areas are governed by agreements signed with local communities and enforced using the authority of the paramount chiefs, section chiefs and village chiefs. Hunting and artisanal mining were widespread in the past but occur now only at very low levels. Surveys of primates since 2012 indicate that, even for taxa that were heavily hunted during armed conflict, populations have returned to similar levels to those observed in the 1980s and – in terms of biomass – are once again among the highest in the world. Protection and management requirements The effective protection and management of the Gola-Tiwai Complex is assured by the National Protected Area Authority of Sierra Leone, which has delegated the day-to-day management of the sites to the not-for-profit Gola Rainforest Conservation company (GRCLG) and the Tiwai Island Administrative Committee. The four directors of the GRCLG include the Government of Sierra Leone, the representatives of two national and international nongovernmental organisations, and an elected representative of the Paramount Chiefs of the seven chiefdoms around GRNP. At both Gola and Tiwai, the close engagement of local communities in the management of the protected areas is key for successful protection. Elsewhere, habitat fragmentation over the past two centuries has left very few large forest blocks intact. Protection and management of GRNP is funded in part by carbon revenues from a Reduced Emissions from Deforestation and Degradation (REDD) project that supports park management as well as the livelihoods of communities in the buffer zone. In addition, major donor agencies have consistently provided financial support for the conservation of the Gola-Tiwai Complex, indicating strong interest on the part of the global conservation community. Monitoring of biodiversity and park management indicators is conducted regularly and will be extended in coming years to include TIWS. Baseline monitoring data on biodiversity and the state of the forest dating back to the 1980s is available for both sites.

sites.name: The Roças of Sao Tome and Principe: Colonial Agricultural System and Forced Migration
sites.short: The serial property comprises six geographically separate roças (Portuguese colonial agricultural plantations) located on the islands of Sao Tome and Principe: Monte Café, Agua Izé, Diogo Vaz, Sao Joao, Sundy, and Belo Monte. Together, they represent a planned colonial plantation system dedicated primarily to coffee and cocoa production, combining agricultural land, industrial infrastructure, residential areas, and social facilities within highly structured spatial layouts. The property illustrates the operation of a large-scale colonial agro-industrial system, based on forced migration and labour, from the late 19th century through the mid-20th century, to sustain global commodity production after the abolition of slavery.

sites.name: The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros
sites.short: The serial property is composed of six historic towns which developed from urban nuclei that emerged around at least the 11th century and evolved into city-states around the 14th-15th century. They eventually became the principal urban centres of the sultanates established on the islands of the archipelago of Comoros. With a common hierarchical system of social organisation, based on matrilineal and matrilocal customs, age-group systems, and patrilineal Islamic traditions still alive today, the property showcases insular urban forms and architectural expressions that resulted from cultural exchanges related to migration and Indian Ocean trade networks, embedded in the local social, geographical, and environmental context.
sites.justification: Brief synthesis The serial property comprises the best-preserved parts of six historic cities located on the islands of Ngazidja and Ndzuwani in the Comoros. They developed from urban nuclei that emerged around at least the 11th century and evolved into city-states around the 14th-15th century, becoming eventually the principal urban centres of the sultanates established in the archipelago of Comoros within the framework of the formation of a Muslim elite linked to the Swahili world. This heritage ensemble, encompassing urban, architectural, and intangible elements, reflects the richness and specificity of Swahili cultural tradition within the Comorian island context. The former sultanic medinas have preserved their old urban morphology and fabric, and an exceptional set of traditions and social practices still alive today. Compact fabrics, with centrally organised palaces and public squares (bangwe, mpangahari), stone houses and defensive structures, the medinas showcase insular urban forms and architectural expressions that resulted from cultural exchanges related to migration and Indian Ocean trade networks, while displaying a spatial logic dictated by a hierarchical system of social organisation based on matrilineal and matrilocal customs, age-group systems, and patrilineal Islamic traditions. The Comorian historic cities, though founded upon the same fundamental cultural and social basis, evolved along distinct trajectories shaped by their geographic, political, social and historical contexts. Criterion (iii): The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros provide an exceptional testimony to the living cultural traditions and social practices of the Comorian archipelago, which, due to its location and complex history, has become a crossroads for peoples of different origins, between Africa, the Arab world, and Europe, connected by the Indian Ocean. The hierarchical social structures of the Comorian society, based on a synthesis of matrilineal and matrilocal customs, age-group system, and patrilineal Islamic traditions, are reflected in the urban organisation of the medinas, which serve as a setting for social life and celebrations that mark the stages of life of men and women, and which in turn give the tangible heritage its meaning. Criterion (iv): The Medinas of the Historic Sultanates of the Comoros constitute a constellation of distinctive responses in architecture and landscape-making that collectively demonstrate the originality of Comorian urban traditions that adapted Arab-Shirazi influences to the local geographic context and combined them with African social structures and models of communal living. Through complementary responses in architecture, artistry, defensive systems, and landscape-making, created within a shared cultural matrix, the component parts showcase the origins and evolution of urbanism in the Comoros, linked to the arrival of Islam, which marked a significant cultural phase in the history of the Indian Ocean region, and illustrates a historical period that witnessed the development of interaction and exchanges between African cultures, the Arab-Muslim world, and various European powers, and the progressive integration of the region into the global maritime context. Integrity While the Comorian medinas of the series share historical and socio-cultural foundations that structure them, the component parts showcase the diversity of architectural, artistic, and planning responses. Each contributes individually to the series through the varying intensities and modalities of external exchanges which, combined with adaptations to specific geographical and insular contexts, generated distinct urban forms and stylistic identities. The component parts include the best-preserved, but sufficiently large, sections of each medina, with the remaining intra-muros areas and some immediate setting comprised within the buffer zones. The serial property retains high integrity in terms of urban morphology, and the system of religious and socio-cultural spaces and centres. However, the oldest built structures (palaces, city walls, historic mosques) are highly vulnerable, with several cases in serious disrepair. The visual interconnections between the cities and the key elements of their natural environment (volcanos, hills, sea), the geographic setting and the maritime connection to the cities are elements that are functionally important as a support to the protection of the property. Authenticity The urban morphology and the spirit of the medinas remain strong in all six component parts, and the authenticity of their use and function is also very high. However, the authenticity of the material fabric of the historic cities has been partly compromised, particularly where concrete reconstructions have been carried out. The gradual loss of traditional skills and massive replacement of materials represent serious threats to the authenticity of the serial property. Historically, the intra-muros sections of the medinas have not been drastically transformed or remodelled, but areas outside the city walls were affected in the modern times. The relationship of the urban centres with the sea is not fully preserved today due to modern developments. Moreover, none of the medinas maintained the maritime commercial context that characterised them during the sultanate era. The intangible heritage still structures the historic cities and gives meaning to the public and private spaces within the medinas. The customary system makes them living spaces of civic and moral education. Protection and management requirements The serial property is protected by Law No. 20-033/AU of 2020 on the Protection of Cultural and Natural Heritage in the Union of the Comoros, promulgated by Presidential Decree no. 21-013/PR. The development within the component parts is regulated by the Urban Planning and Housing Code of 1986, revised in 2011 by Law no. 11-026 on Urban Planning and Construction in the Union of the Comoros. Both legislations need to be supplemented with regulatory texts, which are under preparation. The Framework Law of the Environment no. 94-018, amended in 1995, regulates the landscape environment. Customary, religious, and traditional laws also apply in all component parts. The legislative basis for the creation of a national inventory has been instituted by the establishment of the National Commission for the Protection of Cultural Heritage (CNPPC), responsible for the definition, implementation, and monitoring of the heritage protection policy. This will allow for the registration or listing of the component parts and their enhanced protection at the highest national level, which is yet to be achieved. The National Office for the Valorisation of Heritage (ONVP) is in charge of the mobilisation of funding for the management, valorisation, and tourism promotion. Urban planning instruments (such as Territorial Development Plans (SAT) or Urban Development Plans (PDU)) are either not yet in place or are currently being developed. Four key ministries are involved in the different aspects of management of the serial property: the Ministry of Youth, Employment, Labour, Sports, Arts, and Culture (preservation of historical monuments and sites, their conservation and development); the Ministry of National Education, Teaching, Scientific Research, Training and Professional Integration (scientific research and training); the Ministry of the Environment, responsible for Tourism; and the Ministry of Regional Planning, Urban Development, responsible for Land Affairs and Land Transport. The National Centre for Documentation and Scientific Research (CNDRS), a public scientific and cultural institution, coordinates activities across different stakeholders. The six component parts administratively fall under six municipalities in four prefectures, whose mandate over the serial property is however limited since most of the land is privately owned or is part of the municipal estate. The traditional management system is primarily implemented through the Village Development Committees. The civil society organisations play an active role in the implementation of public policies at the local level and are formally integrated into the management system through the appointment of site managers from among their members. The management plan with an action plan covering the period 2025-2034 is divided into two phases and is being implemented.

sites.name: Village of Sidi Bou Saïd
sites.short: The property is a picturesque village perched on a promontory overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, harmoniously integrated into the cliff topography. It developed around the tomb of a Sufi master and saint, known as Sidi Bou Saïd, who lived in the 12th-13th centuries. Through its architectural fabric and urban planning in symbiosis with the natural environment, its recognisable aesthetic created by emblematic colours, and a mystic aura associated with the Sufi spirituality that permeates the site, the property brings together geomorphology, architecture, and spirituality. It has long inspired artists and continues to attract visitors seeking spiritual serenity.
sites.justification: Brief synthesis The Village of Sidi Bou Saïd is located on top of a hill overlooking the Mediterranean Sea, in northern Tunisia. It developed as a sanctuary-village as a result of a process of aggregation around the mausoleum of a Sufi saint – Abou Saïd Khalaf Ibn Yahya El Tamimi El Beji, known as Sidi Bou Saïd – supported by successive ruling dynasties, which, from the 16th century onwards, fostered the sacralisation of the place by associating their political legitimacy with the baraka (blessing) of the saint. The Husainid beys (18th-20th century) consolidated this dynamic by building holiday residences in Sidi Bou Saïd and turning it into an elite resort. The property embodies the encounter between the spiritual power of the saint and the temporal political power. With the religious complex of Sidi Bou Saïd at its heart, the village reflects the traditional Arab-Islamic urban planning around a central place, enriched by the 19th-20th century urban-type residential architecture of the notables. Criterion (iii): The Village of Sidi Bou Saïd represents an exceptional testimony to the tradition of village foundations based on a symbiotic relationship formed between the spiritual authority of a saint and the temporal power of a ruling dynasty. It exemplifies in an exceptional way the phenomenon of sanctuary-villages, fundamental to the social and political history of the Maghreb, that developed as a result of a saint’s prestige which provided religious legitimacy to the sovereign, and the sovereign’s patronage which, in return, ensured the perpetuation and prosperity of the saint's sanctuary and village. Integrity The property includes the entire historic village of Sidi Bou Saïd, within its 1915 boundaries, excluding a few later buildings which break with the traditional architectural style of the place. The urban morphology and the fabric of the village have been well preserved, and the landscape setting remains largely unaltered, except for the introduction of a marina below the southern slope of the promontory. Other limited instances in which the integrity of the property has been compromised and visual aspects of the site negatively affected are mostly reversible. The site suffers dangerously from instability related to its geological nature and environmental factors. Developmental pressures are largely under control, but excessive tourism is a major concern that requires strategic reorganisation, as it shows to negatively affect the character of the property. At present, despite changes in the socio-cultural and economic context of the site, the vivacity of Sufi spiritual practices persists. Authenticity The property has maintained its morphological coherence and its urban fabric has remained largely unchanged, owing to the 1915 Beylical decree, which helped preserve the village and its historical density. Land division occurred sporadically. The construction of the marina at the southern foot of the promontory modified to a small degree the landscape setting of the property. The mystical practices associated with Sufism remain active and the places of religious practices have mostly retained their original function. The identity of the village that has shaped its history and culture has been maintained, though it faces increasing threats posed by tourism. The related economic dynamics have already led to some changes in the use of residences within the village. Protection and management requirements The property is protected by the Beylical decree of 1915 and the decree 85-1246 of 1985, which provide strong controls against the changes to the spatial organisation of the village, as well as to the fabric and aesthetic of its built environment. The National Institute of Heritage under the Ministry of Cultural Affairs oversees the protection of the property through the Archaeological, Historical and Traditional Arts Heritage Code of 1994. The Institute is also the central body responsible for the management and conservation of the site. The Urban Development Plan for the municipality of Sidi Bou Saïd regulates land uses while incorporating provisions for the protection of heritage, in line with the Territorial and Urban Planning Code of 1994. The management plan has been prepared for a pilot phase (until 2027) and will be further developed.

sites.name: Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape
sites.short: The property comprises Boma National Park, Badingilo National Park, and the surrounding floodplain and savanna landscapes in South Sudan. Located at the interface between the Sudd wetland system and the East Sudanian Savanna, it encompasses an extensive mosaic of seasonally flooded grasslands, wetlands, floodplains, woodlands, and savannas shaped by seasonal rainfall and flood dynamics. These interconnected ecosystems sustain one of the world’s largest remaining terrestrial mammal migrations, with an estimated six million White-eared Kob, Tiang, and Mongalla Gazelle moving across a vast and largely unimpeded landscape in response to changing environmental conditions. The site also reflects important cultural, and linguistic diversity of the region with the Murle, Dinka, Nuer, Anyuak and Toposa and other ethnic groups who have been custodians of this landscape through herding, farming and fishing for centuries and even millennia. The property also supports important populations of numerous large mammal species, including Nile Lechwe, African Savanna Elephant, African Wild Dog, Lion, Leopard, Northeastern Africa Cheetah, and Beisa Oryx, as well as significant assemblages of waterbirds, raptors, and migratory bird species. Its exceptional scale, ecological connectivity, habitat diversity, and relative intactness sustain ecological and biological processes that have become increasingly rare globally.
sites.justification: Brief synthesis The Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape (BBML), covering approximately 11,250,000 hectares in South Sudan, encompasses Boma National Park, Badingilo National Park and the wider floodplain and savanna landscapes that together sustain one of, if not, the world's largest remaining terrestrial mammal migrations. Located at the interface between the Sudd wetland system and the East Sudanian Savanna, the property comprises an extensive mosaic of seasonally flooded grasslands, wetlands, floodplains, woodlands and savannas that support large-scale ecological processes driven by seasonal rainfall and flood dynamics. The property supports the movement of millions of migratory ungulates across a vast and largely unfenced, unimpeded landscape. The migration remains ecologically functional and continues to operate across extensive seasonal habitats and migration corridors, making it one of the last remaining examples of a large-scale terrestrial migration system functioning at a landscape scale. In addition to its migratory wildlife, the property supports important populations of numerous large mammal species, together with significant populations of waterbirds and raptors associated with the floodplain ecosystem. The property's exceptional scale, ecological connectivity and relative intactness underpin ecological and biological processes that have become increasingly rare globally. Criterion (vii): The Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape contains one of, if not, the world's most spectacular remaining wildlife migrations. Each year, an estimate six million White-Eared Kob, Tiang and Mongalla Gazelle move across vast floodplains, wetlands and savannas in response to seasonal flooding and changing resource availability. The scale of the migration, extraordinary numbers of animals involved and the largely intact landscape through which it occurs combine to create an exceptional natural phenomenon of global significance, representing one of the last remaining wildlife spectacles of its kind. Criterion (ix): The Boma–Badingilo Migratory Landscape is an outstanding example of ongoing ecological and biological processes associated with large-scale ungulate migration in a seasonally dynamic savanna ecosystem. The interaction between seasonal flooding, corresponding vegetation productivity and associated wildlife movements sustains what is likely to be the largest remaining terrestrial migration of land mammals in the world. The migration system facilitates ecological connectivity across extensive floodplains, wetlands and grasslands and supports ecological processes that have become increasingly rare as comparable migration systems elsewhere have been fragmented or lost. Criterion (x): The property contains significant habitats for the in-situ conservation of biological diversity, including globally important populations of migratory ungulates and numerous threatened species. The BBML supports globally significant populations of White-Eared Kob, Tiang and Mongalla Gazelle together with important populations of Nile Lechwe, African Savanna Elephant, African Wild Dog, Lion, Leopard, Northeastern Africa Cheetah, Beisa Oryx and other species of conservation importance. The extensive and relatively intact floodplain and savanna ecosystems also provide habitat for important assemblages of waterbirds, raptors and migratory bird species associated with the Upper Nile Basin and migratory flyways. The size, ecological connectivity and habitat diversity of the property contribute significantly to its importance for biodiversity conservation within the East Sudanian Savanna and the greater Nile Basin region. Integrity The property includes the principal migration routes, seasonal habitats, floodplains, wetlands and ecological processes necessary to sustain the large-scale migration system for which it is inscribed. Its exceptional scale and inclusion of the wider migratory landscape are fundamental to the integrity of the property and reflect the ecological reality that the migration system depends upon ecological connectivity across a vast and dynamic landscape. The property retains the key ecological attributes necessary to convey its Outstanding Universal Value, including large migratory wildlife populations, extensive seasonal habitats and relatively intact migration corridors. However, at the time of inscription, the property faces significant threats, including commercial poaching and wildlife trafficking, infrastructure development, insecurity, potential extractive activities, incomplete protection and management arrangements across parts of the wider landscape, and limited institutional and financial capacity. The long-term integrity of the property will depend upon maintaining ecological connectivity, safeguarding migration corridors and seasonal habitats, and ensuring that future development does not adversely affect the ecological processes that underpin Outstanding Universal Value. Protection and management requirements The property includes two legally protected areas, Boma National Park and Badingilo National Park, which provide an important foundation for conservation. The property is managed under the authority of the Ministry of Wildlife Conservation and Tourism and benefits from a management partnership with African Parks. The Wildlife Conservation and Protected Areas Act and other relevant legislation provide the principal legal framework for conservation. The long-term conservation of the property requires a landscape-scale approach to protection and management due to the fact that the ecological processes and migration system that underpin its Outstanding Universal Value are found largely beyond the boundaries of the two national parks. Priority actions, at the time of inscription, include strengthening legal protection within the national parks and across the wider migratory landscape, completing and implementing an integrated landscape-scale land-use and management framework, strengthening consultation, engagement and partnership with Indigenous Peoples and local communities, enhancing management capacity and infrastructure, maintaining ecological connectivity, conserving migration corridors and seasonal habitats, and strengthening governance arrangements for areas outside the existing protected areas. Effective conservation will require sustained investment in law enforcement, ecological monitoring, research, community engagement and institutional capacity, together with measures to address commercial wildlife exploitation, infrastructure development and other pressures affecting the property. The meaningful participation of Indigenous Peoples and local communities in governance, planning and management processes, including through Free, Prior and Informed Consent, will be essential to the long-term conservation of the property's Outstanding Universal Value.
